pos: n. (Flavian of Constantinople, d. 449, archbishop from 446, who condemned Eutyches, received Leo's Tome, and died of the violence done him at the ‘Robber Synod’ of Ephesus)
biblical_def: Flavian presided at the home synod of Constantinople in 448 that examined the monk Eutyches and condemned him for teaching that after the union there was only one nature in Christ, so that His humanity was swallowed up in His deity. Leo of Rome wrote him the letter known as the Tome, which confessed that each nature does what is proper to it in communion with the other, the Word performing what belongs to the Word and the flesh what belongs to the flesh. The confession is Scripture's: “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (Joh 1:14), and “God was manifest in the flesh” (1Ti 3:16), truly God and truly man. At the council of 449, Dioscorus deposed him, and he was so beaten by the soldiers and monks that he died within days on the road to exile. Two years later the Council of Chalcedon honoured him as a martyr and confessed the faith he had defended. He belongs among those of whom Christ said, “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10), and his end fits Paul's: “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines nature as the essence, essential qualities or attributes of a thing, which constitute it what it is.
webster_full: NATURE, n. The essence, essential qualities or attributes of a thing, which constitute it what it is.
2. The established or regular course of things.
3. The constitution and appearances of things.
scriptures: Joh 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
corruption_summary: Flavian died for the distinction of the two natures in Christ, a distinction modern Christians often think too fine to matter and quietly blur.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular piety drifts in both directions Chalcedon forbade: toward a Christ whose humanity is a costume, who did not truly grow, hunger or fear, and toward a Christ who is a uniquely godly man. Both are commonly heard in evangelical teaching on the incarnation, and both were answered by the faith Flavian defended. If Christ's humanity is absorbed, He cannot be our High Priest touched with our infirmities; if His deity is diminished, He cannot save.

The recovery is to learn the Chalcedonian definition and to love it, as the 1689 Confession does in its chapter on Christ the Mediator: two whole, perfect and distinct natures, the Godhead and the manhood, inseparably joined in one Person, without conversion, composition or confusion. Men have been beaten to death for those words.
roots_summary: Greek sarx (G4561), flesh; phaneroo (G5319), to manifest; dioko (G1377), to persecute.
roots_lines: Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh, human nature; John 1:14, 1 Timothy 3:16.
Greek phaneroo (G5319) — to make visible, manifest; 1 Timothy 3:16.
usage: “the Word was made flesh” (Joh 1:14) — the faith Flavian confessed against Eutyches.
“God was manifest in the flesh” (1Ti 3:16) — truly God, truly man.
“I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7) — the end of the archbishop beaten at Ephesus.

pos: n. (Zosimus, d. 418, bishop of Rome 417–418, who first pronounced Pelagius and Celestius orthodox and then, after the African councils and the emperor acted, condemned them)
etymology: Greek Zosimos, from zoe, life, ‘viable, likely to live.’
biblical_def: Zosimus was bishop of Rome for less than two years, and both of the episodes for which he is remembered bear on Rome's claim to an unfailing judgment. When Celestius appealed to him, and Pelagius sent a statement of faith, Zosimus declared them both orthodox and rebuked the African bishops for haste. The Africans did not yield. A council at Carthage in 418 condemned the Pelagian doctrine in canons on original sin and grace, the emperor Honorius banished the Pelagians, and Zosimus then issued a letter condemning the men he had acquitted. In the same months he claimed the right to hear appeals from African clergy, citing canons he called Nicene; when the Africans obtained copies of the Nicene canons from the East, the canons were found to belong to the Council of Sardica. James describes such leadership: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jas 1:8). The church that held firm was the African church, which was not “carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14), and whose heart was “established with grace” (Heb 13:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines appeal as, in law, the removal of a cause or suit from an inferior to a superior judge or court, for re-examination or review.
webster_full: APPEAL, n. In law, the removal of a cause or suit from an inferior to a superior judge or court, for re-examination or review.
2. A summons to answer to a charge.
3. A call upon a person; a reference to another for proof or decision.
scriptures: Jas 1:8
A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.
Eph 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
Heb 13:9
Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines. For it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace; not with meats, which have not profited them that have been occupied therein.
Gal 2:11
But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.
corruption_summary: Zosimus acquitted the Pelagians before he condemned them, and the reversal is a plain historical refutation of the claim that the Roman see has never wavered on the faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Roman apologetics treats Zosimus's final condemnation of Pelagianism as the decisive act, as though the African councils merely waited on Rome. The sequence was the reverse. The bishops of Africa, Augustine among them, held to the Scriptures against the judgment of the pope, and the pope came round. His attempt at the same time to extend his jurisdiction by misattributed canons shows the other habit that would mark the papacy: authority claimed first and justified afterward.

The recovery is the African example. Synods and pastors are bound to test the judgment of any bishop, however eminent, by the Word, and to withstand him to the face when he is to be blamed, as Paul withstood Peter (Gal 2:11). Truth was kept in 418 not by the chair of Peter but by the Scriptures in the hands of faithful men.
roots_summary: Greek dipsuchos (G1374), double minded; kludonizomai (G2831), to be tossed by waves; bebaioo (G950), to establish, confirm.
roots_lines: Greek kludonizomai (G2831) — to be tossed like a wave; Ephesians 4:14.
Greek bebaioo (G950) — to make firm, establish; Hebrews 13:9.
usage: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jas 1:8) — the pope who acquitted and then condemned.
“carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14) — what Africa refused.
“I withstood him to the face” (Gal 2:11) — the precedent the African bishops followed.

pos: n. (John IV of Constantinople, d. 595, patriarch from 582, called the Faster for his austerity, whose use of the title ‘ecumenical patriarch’ Gregory the Great denounced)
etymology: Greek Ioannes Nesteutes, John the Faster, from nesteuo, to fast.
biblical_def: John the Faster was renowned for his abstinence; it was said he lived on almost nothing. As patriarch of the imperial city he used the title ‘ecumenical patriarch,’ and a synod at Constantinople in 587 or 588 applied it to him. Gregory the Great protested in letters to John, to the emperor Maurice and to the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch. He called it a proud and foolish word and a title of blasphemy, and warned that whoever called himself universal priest was in his pride a forerunner of antichrist. Calvin quotes those letters in the Institutes, because within a few years Rome claimed the very thing Gregory had condemned. The irony of John's surname was not lost on Gregory: a man famous for fasting had fallen to pride, as Christ warned of those who fast “that they may appear unto men to fast” (Mat 6:16), and as the Pharisee boasted, “I fast twice in the week” (Luk 18:12). Austerity is no shield against ambition: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Pro 16:18). Christ's rule for His ministers stands: “whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister” (Mar 10:43).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to fast as to abstain from food beyond the usual time; and, religiously, to abstain from food voluntarily as a religious mortification or humiliation.
webster_full: FAST, v.i. To abstain from food, beyond the usual time; to omit to take the usual meals for a time.
2. To abstain from food voluntarily, for the mortification of the body or appetites, or as a token of grief, sorrow and affliction.
scriptures: Mat 6:16
Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister:
corruption_summary: John the Faster's title and Gregory's protest frame the whole later dispute over universal jurisdiction, and both East and West have since claimed what Gregory called the voice of pride.
corruption_paragraphs: The Eastern patriarch of Constantinople still bears the title ‘ecumenical’; the bishop of Rome claims a universal jurisdiction greater than anything John asserted. Each communion remembers the other's pride. Gregory's letters condemn them both, and he wrote them as a bishop of Rome. The modern ecumenical conversation over primacy has to step around his words, because they cannot be reconciled with what either see now claims.

The deeper lesson is about spiritual reputation. A man may be famous for discipline and still be ruled by the love of preeminence; fasting may feed the very pride it was meant to starve. The recovery is Christ's: fast in secret, serve in the open, and let no title in the church lift one brother above the rest.
roots_summary: Greek nesteuo (G3522), to fast; Hebrew ga'on (H1347), pride, arrogance; Greek diakonos (G1249), minister, servant.
roots_lines: Greek nesteuo (G3522) — to abstain from food; Matthew 6:16–18, Luke 18:12.
usage: “that they may appear unto men to fast” (Mat 6:16) — the danger in a famous austerity.
“Pride goeth before destruction” (Pro 16:18) — Gregory's warning in a sentence.
“whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister” (Mar 10:43) — the answer to every universal title.

pos: n. (Ratramnus of Corbie, d. c. 870, Frankish monk whose treatise On the Body and Blood of the Lord denied that the sacramental body is the same as the historical body of Christ; read by Ridley as ‘Bertram’)
etymology: Germanic personal name; English Reformers knew him as Bertram.
biblical_def: Ratramnus was a monk of Corbie in northern France who, about 843, answered two questions put by the king, Charles the Bald: whether the body of Christ in the Supper is present in mystery or in plain truth, and whether it is the same body that was born of Mary, suffered and rose. His abbot Paschasius Radbertus had said yes to the second. Ratramnus said no. The bread and wine, he wrote, are Christ's body and blood in figure and in mystery, received by faith, not the historical body visible to the senses, which is in heaven. He leaned on Augustine and on Christ's own word, “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63), and on the place of the ascended body, “Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things” (Act 3:21). Paul calls the cup and the bread “the communion of the blood of Christ” (1Co 10:16) — a real communion, but by faith and the Spirit. Nicholas Ridley read Ratramnus in the 1540s and was persuaded by him, and through Ridley, Cranmer; the book was printed in English as a witness that the Reformed doctrine was older than Rome's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines figure as the form of any thing as expressed by the outline; and, in theology, a type; a representative.
webster_full: FIGURE, n. The form of any thing as expressed by the outline or terminating extremities.
2. Representation in painting; the lines and colours which represent an animal.
3. In theology, type; representative.
scriptures: Joh 6:63
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
Joh 6:35
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
Act 3:21
Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.
corruption_summary: Ratramnus is the ninth-century proof that Rome's eucharistic doctrine was disputed long before it was defined, and that the Reformers' view had a home inside the medieval church.
corruption_paragraphs: Roman teaching presents the substantial presence of the historical body as the faith of all ages. Ratramnus wrote for a king, in a great abbey, without condemnation in his lifetime, and taught otherwise. His book was put on the Index after the Council of Trent, which is itself a confession that it said what the Reformers claimed it said.

The recovery is not merely antiquarian. The Reformed doctrine of the Supper is not a modern rationalism; it is the faith that Christ's body is in heaven and that believers feed on Him by the Spirit through faith. Ratramnus, Augustine and the Scriptures stand together on that point, and the 1689 Confession confesses it.
roots_lines: Greek apokatastasis (G605) — restoration; Acts 3:21, the only use.
usage: “the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63) — the key Ratramnus took from Christ.
“Whom the heaven must receive” (Act 3:21) — where the historical body is.
“the communion of the blood of Christ” (1Co 10:16) — real communion, by faith.

pos: n. (Paschasius Radbertus, c. 790–c. 865, abbot of Corbie, whose treatise On the Body and Blood of the Lord taught that the Eucharistic body is the very flesh born of Mary, the first full statement of the doctrine later called transubstantiation)
etymology: Latin Paschasius, from pascha, Passover; Germanic Radbert, bright counsel.
biblical_def: Paschasius Radbertus wrote the first treatise devoted wholly to the Supper, about 831, for the monks of a daughter house of Corbie, and revised it for Charles the Bald in 844. He taught that by the power of God the substance of the bread and wine becomes the very flesh that was born of Mary, suffered on the cross and rose from the tomb, though hidden under the outward appearance, and he told miracle stories of hosts that bled. He pressed Christ's words, “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you” (Joh 6:53), in the most literal sense, and passed over the same discourse's key, “the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63). Rabanus Maurus and his own monk Ratramnus answered him. His view did not prevail at once, but it supplied the substance of what the Fourth Lateran Council defined in 1215. Hebrews closes the door his doctrine opened, since Christ “needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice” (Heb 7:27), but “was once offered to bear the sins of many” (Heb 9:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines substance as that which exists by itself; that which really is or exists; and, in theology, the essential part of a thing.
webster_full: SUBSTANCE, n. In a general sense, being; something existing by itself; that which really is or exists.
2. That which supposes something underlying all outward appearances.
3. The essential part; the main or material part.
scriptures: Joh 6:53
Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.
Joh 6:63
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
Heb 7:27
Who needeth not daily, as those high priests, to offer up sacrifice, first for his own sins, and then for the people's: for this he did once, when he offered up himself.
Heb 9:28
So Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many; and unto them that look for him shall he appear the second time without sin unto salvation.
corruption_summary: Paschasius gave the medieval church its doctrine of the altar, and with it the miracle stories, the elevation and the adoration that turned the Supper into a spectacle.
corruption_paragraphs: The move Paschasius made was to identify the sacramental body with the historical body, so that what lies on the altar is the flesh of Mary's Son. From that identification followed, over three centuries, the adoration of the host, the elevation at the words of institution, the reservation in tabernacles, the processions, and the sacrifice of the mass offered for the living and the dead. A sign appointed to be eaten became an object to be looked at and worshipped.

The Reformed answer, given by the 1689 Confession, is that the Supper is not a sacrifice offered to the Father but a commemoration of the one offering of Christ, and that the doctrine of a change of substance overthrows the nature of the ordinance and is the cause of manifold superstitions and gross idolatries. The recovery is the table as Christ set it: bread to be taken and eaten in remembrance of Him.
roots_summary: Greek trogo (G5176), to eat; hapax (G530), once; prosphero (G4374), to offer.
roots_lines: Greek hapax (G530) — once, once for all; Hebrews 9:28, 7:27 (ephapax).
usage: “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man” (Joh 6:53) — the text Paschasius read literally.
“the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63) — the key he passed over.
“So Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many” (Heb 9:28) — why the altar has no sacrifice.

pos: n. (Lanfranc of Bec, c. 1005–1089, Italian monk, prior of Bec in Normandy, chief opponent of Berengar on the Supper, and archbishop of Canterbury under William the Conqueror from 1070)
etymology: Germanic personal name, from land, land, and frank, free. Teacher of Anselm at Bec.
biblical_def: Lanfranc was a lawyer from Pavia who became a monk at Bec, made its school the most famous in Europe, and taught Anselm there. He was Berengar's principal opponent, and his treatise On the Body and Blood of the Lord argued that the earthly substances are changed into the essence of the Lord's body while their outward appearance remains — the vocabulary that became transubstantiation. He used the new tools of logic against his opponent while accusing him of trusting reason too much. Christ's words of institution were plain enough to need no such apparatus: “Take, eat; this is my body” (Mat 26:26), and the same evening, “this do in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:24), so that the Supper is to “shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26). William the Conqueror made him archbishop of Canterbury in 1070, and he reorganised the English church on the Norman pattern, tying it more closely to Rome. Paul's rule for every minister judges his method as well as his matter: “not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully” (2Co 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines logic as the art of thinking and reasoning justly; the science of the operations of the understanding subservient to the estimation of evidence.
webster_full: LOGIC, n. The art of thinking and reasoning justly.
2. The science of the operations of the understanding, subservient to the estimation of evidence.
scriptures: And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body.
And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.

But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
corruption_summary: Lanfranc defended a literal reading of ‘this is my body’ with Aristotle's categories, and the result was a doctrine that needs philosophy to state and contradicts the senses to believe.
corruption_paragraphs: Transubstantiation is often defended as simple faith in Christ's words. In its history it was the opposite: a technical construction in which the accidents of bread remain while the substance changes, worked out by Lanfranc and refined by the schoolmen with categories borrowed from Aristotle. The plain sense of a sacramental saying — that the bread is His body as a sign is the thing it signifies, in the manner Scripture uses everywhere for covenant signs — was set aside for a metaphysical miracle.

The recovery is to read the words of institution as Scripture reads its own signs. Circumcision is called the covenant; the lamb is called the Passover; the cup is called the new testament. The Supper is Christ's body given and blood shed, set forth to faith, and the believer needs no categories to receive Him there.
roots_summary: Greek eulogeo (G2127), to bless; klao (G2806), to break; panourgia (G3834), craftiness.
roots_lines: Greek eulogeo (G2127) — to bless, give thanks; Matthew 26:26.
Greek klao (G2806) — to break bread; Matthew 26:26, 1 Corinthians 11:24.
usage: “Take, eat; this is my body” (Mat 26:26) — the words Lanfranc defended with logic.
“this do in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:24) — the same night, the same Lord.
“nor handling the word of God deceitfully” (2Co 4:2) — the minister's rule.

pos: n. (Jean Gerson, 1363–1429, chancellor of the University of Paris, leading conciliarist at the Council of Constance, which ended the Great Schism and burned John Hus)
etymology: French, from the village of Gerson in Champagne where he was born; his family name was Charlier.
biblical_def: Gerson was the most influential theologian of the early fifteenth century. The Western church had two popes and then three, each excommunicating the others, and Gerson argued that a general council holds its authority directly from Christ and may judge, depose and replace a pope. At Constance the decree Haec Sancta (1415) declared exactly that, and the council deposed the rival claimants and elected Martin V. Gerson appealed to the apostolic pattern: “the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6), and to Christ's word, “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17). Solomon's maxim was his whole theory: “in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14). Yet the same council, with Gerson's energetic support, condemned John Hus and burned him in 1415 despite the emperor's safe-conduct, and condemned the teaching of Wycliffe. Conciliarism restrained the pope but did not return the church to Scripture as its rule; the council itself claimed to speak as the Spirit, “it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us” (Act 15:28), without the apostles' warrant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines council as an assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice; and, in church history, an assembly of prelates and doctors convened for regulating matters of doctrine and discipline.
webster_full: COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
2. An assembly of prelates and doctors, convened for regulating matters of doctrine and discipline in the church.
3. Act of public deliberation; consideration.
scriptures: Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;
corruption_summary: Gerson's conciliarism is sometimes hailed as a step toward the Reformation; it moved supreme authority from one bishop to an assembly of bishops, and that assembly burned Hus.
corruption_paragraphs: Historians often present the conciliar movement as the medieval church's own reform, a constitutional check on papal monarchy and a forerunner of Protestant liberty. It did check the pope for a generation, and Rome soon reversed it. But its principle was that the church, gathered in council, is the final judge of faith, which is not the Reformation principle at all. Constance claimed an authority over conscience as absolute as any pope's, and used it against a man who appealed to Scripture.

The 1689 Confession states the Reformed answer: synods and councils may err and many have erred, and their decisions are to be received with reverence only if they agree with the Word of God. Authority does not become safe by being shared among many; it becomes safe by being bound to Scripture.
roots_summary: Greek presbuteros (G4245), elder; ekklesia (G1577), church, assembly; Hebrew ya'ats (H3289), to counsel.
usage: “the apostles and elders came together” (Act 15:6) — the pattern Gerson appealed to.
“in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14) — the conciliar theory in a proverb.
“it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us” (Act 15:28) — an apostolic warrant no later council inherits.

pos: n. (Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, c. 345–402, pagan senator and prefect of Rome, who pleaded in 384 for the restoration of the Altar of Victory and recommended Augustine for the chair of rhetoric at Milan)
etymology: Greek summachos, ally, fellow-fighter. Not to be confused with Symmachus the second-century translator of the Old Testament, or the later Pope Symmachus.
biblical_def: Symmachus was the most eloquent pagan of his generation and the leader of the senators who held to the old gods. When the emperor Gratian removed the Altar of Victory from the senate house, Symmachus, as prefect of the city, petitioned the young Valentinian II in 384 to restore it. His plea became famous for one sentence: that not by one road only can men come to so great a mystery. Ambrose answered him in two letters, and the altar was not restored. The gospel's answer is Christ's: “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6), and Peter's: “Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12). The first commandment had settled it at Sinai: “Thou shalt have no other gods before me” (Exo 20:3). In the same year Symmachus chose the young African Augustine, then still a Manichee, for the post of rhetor at Milan, and so sent him, without knowing it, to sit under Ambrose. Elijah's question hung over his whole career: “How long halt ye between two opinions?” (1Ki 18:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plurality as a number consisting of two or more of the same kind; and, in the church, the holding of two or more benefices by one clergyman.
webster_full: PLURALITY, n. A number consisting of two or more of the same kind.
2. A state of being or having a greater number.
3. In the church, the holding of two or more benefices by the same clergyman.
scriptures: Joh 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
Exo 20:3
Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word.
corruption_summary: ‘Not by one road’ is the creed of religious pluralism, and Symmachus stated it more gracefully in 384 than any modern interfaith declaration has managed.
corruption_paragraphs: Symmachus's argument has every modern note: the antiquity of the traditions, respect for the ancestors, the mystery too great for any one path, and the request for public space for all religions. It is now the default of Western culture and the working assumption of much liberal Christianity, which treats Christ as one way among many to a divine mystery. It sounds humble. It is a denial that God has spoken.

Ambrose's answer was that Christians cannot sanction an altar to a false god in the place where they are called to serve the true one; the gospel's exclusive claim is not arrogance but the content of the message. The providence in the story is the other half of the recovery. The man who pleaded for many roads sent Augustine down the one road that leads to the Father.
roots_summary: Greek hodos (G3598), way, road; Hebrew pasach (H6452), to halt, limp; Greek soteria (G4991), salvation.
usage: “no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6) — the answer to ‘not by one road.’
“none other name under heaven” (Act 4:12) — the exclusive gospel.
“How long halt ye between two opinions?” (1Ki 18:21) — Elijah to every Symmachus.

pos: n. (Possidius of Calama, d. after 437, bishop of Calama in Numidia, Augustine's friend of forty years and author of the first Life of Augustine)
etymology: Latin personal name. His Life is followed by a catalogue (Indiculum) of Augustine's writings.
biblical_def: Possidius was a member of Augustine's monastic household at Hippo before he became bishop of Calama, and he remained Augustine's companion in controversy against Donatists and Pelagians for nearly forty years. He wrote the Life of Augustine soon after his friend's death, and its last chapters are a plain record of how a Christian died. Augustine lay ill in Hippo in August 430 while the Vandals besieged the city. He had the penitential psalms of David copied out and fixed on the wall where he could see them from his bed, and read them, weeping. They had always been his songs: “For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me” (Psa 51:3). He asked that no one should visit him for his last ten days except at the hours when the physicians came or food was brought, so that he might give himself to prayer. Possidius was with him, and his book is an act of the duty Hebrews enjoins: “Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation” (Heb 13:7). Like Paul, Augustine could say, “the time of my departure is at hand” (2Ti 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines biography as the history of the life and character of a particular person.
webster_full: BIOGRAPHY, n. The history of the life and character of a particular person.
scriptures: Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
Psa 51:3
For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.
For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand.
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
corruption_summary: Possidius's account of Augustine's death — a great theologian weeping over the penitential psalms — contradicts both the modern triumphalist deathbed and the modern assumption that assurance and repentance cannot live together.
corruption_paragraphs: The Christian biographies of our day prefer achievement: what a man built, how many he reached, what he left behind. Possidius records books and controversies, but the scene he lingers on is a bishop, after forty years of service, reading David's confessions of sin and weeping. A culture that treats self-esteem as health cannot understand that scene, and some Christians suspect it of doubt. It was neither despair nor doubt; it was the humility of a man who knew he would stand before God on grace alone.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Possidius served: remember the faithful, consider the end of their conversation, and follow their faith. A church that preserves the memory of how its fathers died will die better itself.
roots_summary: Greek mnemoneuo (G3421), to remember; ekbasis (G1545), end, outcome; Hebrew yada' (H3045), to know, acknowledge.
roots_lines: Greek mnemoneuo (G3421) — to call to mind, remember; Hebrews 13:7.
usage: “considering the end of their conversation” (Heb 13:7) — why Possidius wrote.
“my sin is ever before me” (Psa 51:3) — the psalm on Augustine's wall.
“So teach us to number our days” (Psa 90:12) — the lesson of the deathbed at Hippo.

pos: n. (Gelasius I, d. 496, bishop of Rome from 492, whose letter on the two powers shaped medieval church-state theory and whose decree against dividing the sacrament the Reformers cited against communion in one kind)
etymology: Greek Gelasios, from gelao, to laugh. An African by birth, according to the Liber Pontificalis.
biblical_def: Gelasius is remembered for two texts. In a letter of 494 to the emperor Anastasius he wrote that there are two powers by which this world is chiefly ruled, the sacred authority of the priests and the royal power, and that the priests' charge is the weightier because they must answer even for kings at the judgment. Medieval popes stretched that letter into a claim of supremacy over princes, but its own distinction is closer to Christ's: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21), with the magistrate as “the minister of God to thee for good” (Rom 13:4). His second text is a decree preserved in Gratian's Decretum. Some at Rome, from Manichaean scruple, received the bread and refused the cup. Gelasius ordered that they either receive the whole sacrament or be kept from the whole, because the division of one and the same mystery cannot be made without great sacrilege. The Reformers quoted it against Rome's later practice of withholding the cup from the people. Christ had said of the cup, “Drink ye all of it” (Mat 26:27), and Paul delivered it to the whole church: “this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sacrilege as the crime of violating or profaning sacred things; the alienating to laymen or to common purposes what has been appropriated or consecrated to religious persons or uses.
webster_full: SACRILEGE, n. The crime of violating or profaning sacred things; or the alienating to laymen or to common purposes what has been appropriated or consecrated to religious persons or uses.
scriptures: And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it;
After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.
They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
corruption_summary: A pope called the dividing of the sacrament sacrilege; the later Roman church withheld the cup from the laity for centuries, and the Council of Trent anathematised those who said the practice was wrong.
corruption_paragraphs: The withdrawal of the cup grew up in the high Middle Ages out of reverence for the blood and fear of spilling it, and the Council of Constance made it law in 1415, the same council that burned Hus, whose followers demanded the cup. Trent defended it. Gelasius's decree stood in Rome's own canon law the whole time, condemning the thing Rome did. Calvin and the Reformers did not need to invent the argument; they quoted the pope.

The recovery is the table as Christ furnished it, with bread and cup for every communicant. The 1689 Confession names the denial of the cup to the people as contrary to the nature of the ordinance and to the institution of Christ. Reverence does not consist in keeping from the people what the Lord commanded them to take.
roots_lines: Greek poterion (G4221) — a drinking vessel, cup; Matthew 26:27, 1 Corinthians 11:25.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — servant, minister, used of the magistrate; Romans 13:4.
usage: “Drink ye all of it” (Mat 26:27) — the command Gelasius would not see divided.
“this do ye, as oft as ye drink it” (1Co 11:25) — the cup delivered to the whole church.
“unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21) — the truth inside the letter on the two powers.
